---
title: "Index separators"
filters:
  - index
---

An index prints punctuation its author never writes: a mark between a term and
its locators, another between one locator and the next, and a third between two
cross-references filed on one term. English print convention makes the first
two a comma and the third a semicolon. This document and its twin write the
same marks and differ only in whether the metadata above declares those two
marks — so what a reader sees here is whatever that metadata says, and the
English punctuation wherever it says nothing.

A declaration sets the glyph alone. The space after it is this extension's, so
a value written without one cannot glue a locator to the term in front of it.

Nothing below declares punctuation. Every mark here is an ordinary one, and the
four entries between them reach every position an index prints punctuation at.

## Two locators on one term {#site-first}

A term marked once here — [Azurite]{.index} — and again on the page below, so
its entry carries two locators, with punctuation between them as well as in
front of them.

{{< pagebreak >}}

The second mark on that term: [Azurite]{.index}.

## A term with both a locator and a cross-reference {#site-second}

A term marked plainly, [Beryl]{.index}, and marked again pointing further on:
[Beryl]{.index see-also="Azurite"}. Its entry prints a locator and then a
cross-reference, so punctuation stands in front of each.

## Cross-references with no locator {#site-third}

A term that is only a pointer, so the first punctuation its entry prints stands
between the term and the cross-reference: [Cinnabar]{.index see="Azurite"}.

A term that is two pointers, marked once for each, which is the one place the
cross-reference punctuation is printed: [Dolomite]{.index see="Azurite"} and
[Dolomite]{.index see-also="Beryl"}.
